query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of Silicon (Si) into equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will induce the formation of a continuous, dense SiO2-enriched subsurface layer during high-temperature exposure, thereby preventing pesting and catastrophic oxidation without significantly degrading the room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a BCC solid solution structure, exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but suffering from inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) in air.
generation.intervention: Addition of a trace amount (e.g., 0.5–2.0 at.%) of Silicon (Si) to the alloy composition prior to casting.
generation.conditions: Isothermal exposure in air at 800 °C to 1000 °C for durations up to 100 hours; subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature and 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, continuous, and adherent SiO2-rich oxide scale that forms preferentially over the HfO2/TiO2/NbO2 matrix, acting as a diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: Silicon has a high affinity for oxygen and lower volatility compared to Hf and Ti oxides at intermediate temperatures. The addition of Si promotes the nucleation of a protective SiO2 layer (or Si-enriched mixed oxide) that seals surface defects and prevents the rapid inward diffusion of oxygen that causes pesting (catastrophic spalling and disintegration), while the low concentration of Si avoids the formation of brittle intermetallic phases that typically degrade mechanical properties in Al/Cr/Si-doped RHEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Si-doped alloy will exhibit a transition from exponential (pesting) to parabolic oxidation kinetics at 800–1000 °C, with negligible mass gain compared to the untreated alloy. Room-temperature ductility will remain >8% and high-temperature yield strength will be preserved within 10% of the baseline, unlike Al/Cr-doped variants which suffer from brittle intermetallic formation.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, which exhibits catastrophic pesting (rapid disintegration) and exponential weight gain during air exposure at 800 °C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to trace Si additions (<2 at.%); higher Si concentrations are expected to form brittle silicide intermetallics (e.g., HfSi2, Ti5Si3) that would violate the mechanical performance constraint. The protection is effective in air up to 1000 °C but may degrade above 1100 °C if SiO2 volatilization becomes significant.
generation.uncertainty: While Al and Cr are known to form protective oxides, they form brittle intermetallics in this system (PMC10142552). Si is theoretically superior for oxidation resistance but its specific interaction with the HfNbTaTiZr matrix to avoid brittle phase formation at trace levels is not explicitly confirmed in the provided evidence, creating uncertainty regarding the exact threshold for mechanical property retention.

falsification_experiment.design: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 1.0 at.% Si and a control sample of pure HfNbTaTiZr. Expose both to air at 800 °C for 50 hours. Perform tensile testing at room temperature and 1000 °C on the oxidized samples.
measurements: Isothermal thermogravimetric analysis (weight gain vs. time) to determine oxidation kinetics (parabolic vs. exponential).
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) of the oxide scale to identify SiO2 enrichment and scale continuity.
Room temperature tensile ductility (elongation to fracture) and yield strength at 1000 °C.
X-ray Diffraction (XRD) to detect brittle intermetallic phases (e.g., silicides) in the bulk.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) the Si-doped sample exhibits exponential weight gain or catastrophic pesting similar to the baseline; OR (2) the Si-doped sample shows a >20% reduction in room-temperature ductility or >20% reduction in high-temperature yield strength compared to the baseline, indicating the formation of detrimental brittle intermetallics.
